record.title: Integrating Model-Based Systems Engineering and Value-Based Design with an NEA Scout Small Satellite Example
record.abstract: There has recently been a tremendous growth in the use of model - ba sed systems engineering (MBSE) among different categories of practitioners including government, industry, and academia. MBSE aims at using a consistent system model that is updated throughout the system life cycle to form a digital twin, to enable improv ed decision - making. OMG’s Systems Modeling Language (SysML) is one of the primary modeling languages used to model not only system hardware and software, but also the people and processes involved in system development. SysML is finding increased applicati on in different sectors, and is gaining favor among practitioners for their modeling needs. Value - based design (VBD) mathematically represents the preference of the stakeholder in the form of a value model which can be maximized to determine the optimal sy stem. This paper attempts to bring together the benefits of SysML and value modeling to enable more informed decisions. This is performed by integrating value models with SysML to evaluate and compare alternatives. The challenges to integrating the two ap proaches are discussed and an example of the NEA Scout cube satellite modeled in Cameo Enterprise Architecture with stakeholder preference represented mathematically in a value model is used to explore the topic.

record.title: Mathematical Representation of Stakeholder Preferences for the SPORT Small Satellite Project
record.abstract: The design of complex systems involves mu ltiple stakeholders with various preferences working together to realize a single system . Th e interfaces existing between the subsystems creates a complex system in itself. While contributing to the same system, design teams have unique objectives to their team and the subsystem they are designing. T he preferences of individuals within each design team may also be unique , adding to the overall pro ject complexity . Differing preferences often lead to challenges in many aspects of systems engineering, such as leadership, project management, contracting and interface documentation . This paper is a first step to overcome such challenges by understanding the impac t of differing preferences on system design. The aim of the paper will be to mathematically represen t a small satellite system’s stakeholders’ preferences using value models based on general beliefs about organizational goals . Specific to this study, stakeholders represent various organizations , both in the top management level as well as design teams de veloping the subsystems for t he Scintillation Prediction Observation Research Task ( SPORT ). Four value models were created to represent the preferences of stakeholders involved in the SPORT project. The attributes affecting these differing preferences were identified, and the expected implication of these attributes on the satellite design was discussed. While the value models depict preference that were specific to each organization, similarities of p references amongst stakeholders could also be found. Fut ure work will compare the presented value models to value models generated by the stakeholders through survey research .

record.title: The Role of V&V in the Early Stages of the Lifecycle
record.abstract: Verification and Validation (V&V) activities typically occur in the later phases of the system lifecycle. Verification activities focus on developing evidence that we “built the system right,” that the system meets its design. Validation activities ensure that we “built the right system,” that it delivers the capabilities intended for stakeholders. This paper discusses how to use the techniques of V&V, including simulation, early in the lifecycle to enhance the probability of success of the program by identifying errors early in the development and preparing for the V&V activities later in the lifecycle.

record.title: Design of a Zero-Gravity, Vacuum-Based 3D Printer Robot for Use of In-Space Satellite Assembly
record.abstract: Additive manufacturing has revolutionized many industries through its ability to print unique architectures impossible to create with traditional subtractive manufacturing. The space environment, given its condition of microgravity and vacuum, creates unique challenges for most additive methods, but also an exceptional opportunity. This paper explores the application of additive manufacturing (or 3D printing) in this new environment, and introduces design opportunities for a printing robot for such application of satellite assembly on-orbit. The ability to print both long, simple booms and large, flat structures like an antenna dish will be pursued. This capability will help reduce structural limitations due to the launch environment and allow for unique satellite architectures outside the boundaries of a launch vehicle payload fairing. From a systems engineering viewpoint, the mission and system requirements and initial design specifications will be discussed and integration of the 3D printer capability on the robot will detailed.

record.title: BEST-NG : a new modeler for describing the satellite?s database
record.abstract: As the BEST engineering tooling https://logiciels.cnes.fr/content/best ) is no longer adapted to the requirements of new space projects (in terms of data size and data formats), the CNES ( ) is preparing a new generation of software to replace this framework. This paper presents the BEST-NG solution, a new modeling editor for des cribing the content of the satellite’s database. BEST -NG is designed to address multi- domain issues and multi-format issues: in a single model, it can handle information from XTCE, CADS, XIF M&C, and XIF files. The solution is based on a UML-like custom Profile approach and the use of EMF Facet. It uses Eclipse Modeling technologies to solve major challenges. Especially, it provides import/export support for all these formats, good performances, validation, and a rich user-friendly expressions editor — implemented with Xtext — . BEST-NG should be used as the corner stone for future developments concerning the new space database management tools suite developed for the CNES.

record.title: The Sentinels LEOP Experience: Putting in Orbit the Copernicus Constellation
record.abstract: The Copernicus Program (formerly kno wn as GMES or Global Monitoring for Environment and Security) is a EU - driven program whose main objective is to s upport Europe’s goals regarding sustainable development and global governance of the environment by providing timely and quality data, informat ion, services and knowledge. ESOC - Darmstadt is the responsible for the Launch and Early Orbit Phases (LEOP) of the first set of Sentinels (namely Sentinel - 1A/B, - 2A/B, - 3A/B, - 5P and - 6) , encompassing the procurement, set - up, test, integration, validatio n and execution of the Flight Operations Segment (FOS) required to implement the above LEOP operations. This paper describe s the assumptions and concepts that were considered within the Flight Operations Segment when defining the different requirements, limitations and constraints linked to the LEOP operations of the Sentinels. The paper present s how the selected concept and infrastructure allowed for a smooth LEOP FOS design where new Sentinels missions could prepare their LEOP operations re - using the av ailable components, reducing testing, integration and validation time, in parallel to executing their nominal operations. The resulting LEOP Operational Concept applied across the Sentinels’ is summarized, including the as - executed LEOP results, highlighti ng the lessons learnt , achieved efficiencies/cost reductions, and the evolutions for the upcoming Sentinels .

record.title: Reliability Model Supporting Satellite Life Extension and Disposal Operations Initiation
record.abstract: This paper presents on-going R&D activities aiming at deriving an improved reliability model enabling a more accurate quantitative risk assessment and at defining decision- making criteria for the execution of end of life disposal or a possible life extension. In this sense, a process no longer based only on consumables but also on a reliability criterion is investigated. The final goal is to be able to dispose the satellite at end of life in a safer and more reliable manner even in case of failures. This will in turn allow to limit the proliferation of space debris in already crowded Low Earth Orbits and to be fully compliant to international Space Debris Mitigation standards and specific applicable regulations (e.g. French Law : LOS “ Lois des Opérations Spatiales ” ).

record.title: Agile Mission Operations in the CubeSat Project MOVE-II
record.abstract: With the continuous advancements in commercial oﬀ-the-shelf small satellite technology, there has been a signiﬁcant increase in proposed missions and an ongoing trend towards rapid development and launch. Traditionally, mission operations of larger spacecraft utilize established products, adapting the operational interfaces and software to the needs of the speciﬁc mission. This paper reports the creation of the mission operations interface for a CubeSat mission from scratch to a fully operational system in about seven months under the voluntary commitment of about six students. We will ﬁrst give a short introduction into the traditional software development used extensively in the space sector before we brieﬂy describe CubeSats and our own CubeSat project, called MOVE-II. The used software development process will be described using the agile methodology Scrum as a baseline. It will be explained how this process was implemented utilizing tools like Trello, GitLab and Slack. Afterward the software design, as well as used frameworks and software, are brieﬂy described to demonstrate how these go hand in hand with our development process. Subsequently, our operations software, as well as satellite operations with our software, are described with a focus on advantages and disadvantages of our software development approach and general lessons learned that we gathered during our project.

record.title: Small Satellite Deorbital System using Magnetic Field Controlled Plasma
record.abstract: Space Debris is one of the major challenges for the Aerospace community today. The presence of decommissioned satellites as well as rocket bodies from old missions has led to the overpopulation of the Lower Earth Orbit and Geostationary Orbit to the point that it has become a safety hazard for satellites in operation as well as a massive obstruction to future missions. In order to completely access the space infrastructure, space debris management is necessary. The focus of this paper is constricted to small debris particles in the Lower Earth Orbit which are relatively harder to catalogue and can cause fatal damages to the satellites in the orbit. Since the removal of existing debris is not feasible at the moment, we can ensure the prevention of creation of more debris in the future by an efficient de-orbital system for the small satellites. The main problem related to end-of-life manoeuvres of small satellites is that their low area-to-mass ratio makes them insusceptible to already-low atmospheric drag. The satellites are only dependant on a reserve propellant which itself adds to the cost of the mission. Therefore, we require an economical, lightweight, fuel-less system that can be easily integrated to small satellites and decelerate them at a controlled rate so that they can be safely deorbited. The plasma particles present in upper atmosphere are known to have a destabilizing effect on orbiting satellites. In the lower atmosphere, the drag effect of plasma increases due to its interaction with the surrounding neutral particles of the atmosphere. Thus, the effect of plasma combined with geomagnetism can be tapped to provide a small decelerating effect to the small satellites in LEO. The paper shall focus on the design and development of such a system that can deorbit the satellite safely in less than 10 years and ensure that it does not cause any hindrance to operation of other satellites.

record.title: High Altitude Aerodynamic Reflectors To Counter Climate Change
record.abstract: The warming of the atmosphere by net radiative forcing is now estimated to exceed 2.92 Watts per square meter of Earth’s surface. Present eﬀorts to reduce emissions of greenhouse gases and waste heat are insuﬃcient to reduce the rate of increase of radiative forcing, let alone reverse it. We discuss one implementation of an incremental, reversible and controlled concept to directly reduce heat input to the atmosphere. Swarms of thin reﬂective sheets are aerodynamically ﬂoated and controlled above 28 kilometers altitude using solar-powered electric-propelled tractor wings. The swarms drift with the summer latitudes year-round. They stay well above controlled airspace even through the longest nocturnal altitude loss of equatorial crossing. Building on prior work, wind tunnel tests study passive stabilization of thin sheets. The sheet is restrained using two edge rails and aft control surface mounted on canted vertical ﬁns. The deployment process is updated. The sheet angle of attack has to be raised to counter wing suction. Means of distributing sheet loading are studied. Passive sheet stabilization is demonstrated, with 20 micron shrink-wrap plastic, and 175-micron Mylar sheets surviving dynamic pressures an order of magnitude higher than the design cruise condition. Scaling surface imperfections is a hurdle in proving drag predictions in these wind tunnel tests at full- scale Reynolds number. The second part of the paper derives and proposes an equivalence in carbon credits between reduction of atmospheric greenhouse gases, and avoidance of heat input to the atmosphere. The proposed architecture passes all known objections warning against Climate Engineering.

record.title: Methodology and Tools for Reducing CubeSat Mission Failure
record.abstract: A CubeSat is considered a great engineering system used for space research in the last decade. This is due to its simple design, low cost, and usage of open - source software and hardware tools. CubeSats are in high demand for use in a multitude of ways. Universities invest in space studies by encouraging and educating STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Math) students to be i nvolved in designing, implementing, and testing of CubeSats. Universities differ in their CubeSat missions. A 1U CubeSat can be launched into space and operate on a simple mission for basic science experiments. CubeSats can also be deployed in clusters for space exploration. According to Swartwout, however, roughly 50% of CubeSats fail to fulfill their mission. Different reasons lead CubeSats to fail including power, mechanical, and communication issues. Some researchers suggested for this high level of fa ilure, that universities and research institutions mainly focus on the system and component level design, while neglecting the elicitation of requirements needed beforehand. To minimize the rate of failure of CubeSat missions, this research proposes a fram ework for CubeSat systems engineering. This system provides tools to help institutions with planning, collecting, elicitation, and documenting requirements in a well - defined manner. This paper focuses on universities’ CubeSat projects designed by students and faculty members. Thus, a recent survey has been conducted by the researcher to identify the challenges and needs of such groups. Plans for future work are also discussed.

record.title: Developing an MBSE CubeSat Reference Model ? Interim Status #4
record.abstract: Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) is the formalized application of modeling to support systems engineering. The International Council on Systems Engineering (INCOSE) Space Systems Working Group (SSWG) has been investigating the applicability of MBSE for designing CubeSats by developing a CubeSat Reference Model (CRM). The CRM is intended for instruction and for designing and building a mission-specific CubeSat. Additionally, we are collaborating with Object Management Group (OMG) Space Domain Task Force (SDTF) to develop the CRM as an OMG specification. Our application of MBSE utilizes the Systems Modeling Language (SysML) a graphical modeling language . This paper presents reports on the maturation of the CRM including: 1) CRM as an OMG specification, 2) expansion of architecture and requirement packages to component level, 3) population of architecture and requirement packages using table-based user interfaces, 4) incorporation of technical measures and use cases, and 5) CRM validation strategy.

record.title: SysML Output Interface and System-Level Requirement Analyzer for the Horizon Simulation Framework
record.abstract: Model-Based Systems Engineering in industry has been constantly increasing its presence within the aerospace industry. SysML is one such MBSE tool that shows complex system organization and relationships. The Horizon Simulation Framework is another MBSE tool, created by Cal Poly researcher, that gives users the ability to run “day-in-the-life” simulations of systems. Finding a way to link these two tools could allow systems engineers to reap the benefits of both. This paper investigates the background and design process involved with developing the code that can convert an output file generated in SysML, into a format specifically made for the Horizon Simulation Framework. The goal was to create an interface that can allow users to model a system in SysML, and analyze the model and verify system requirements using HSF. Another goal was to expand the capabilities of the Horizon Simulation Framework by designing and develop a module that would allow users to define and analyze system-level requirements. To evaluate the effectiveness of both codes, the Aeolus example case was used. A SysML model of the system was created as the product of other work; SysML based CubeSat Model Design and Integration with the Horizon Simulation Framework. The Aeolus SysML model was converted and used as input in an HSF simulation. The SysML model simulation data was compared against those of the original test case. To test the requirement module, system level requirements were formulated within the Aeolus system and run in simulation, providing an analysis of the results. The results of the analysis confirmed a successful conversion of the SysML model into an equivalent HSF model and a successful analysis of system-level requirements.

record.title: Extended Orbital Flight of a CubeSat in the Lower Thermosphere with Active Attitude Control
record.abstract: A wide variety of scientifically interesting missions could be enabled by orbital flight altitudes of 150 – 250 km. This range of altitudes is defined as extremely Low Earth Orbit (eLEO) for the present work. The use of low-cost nanosatellites (mass < 10 kg) has reduced the cost barrier to orbital flight over the last decade and the present study investigates the feasibility of using primarily commercial, off-the-shelf (COTS) hardware to build a nanosat specifically to allow extended mission times in eLEO. The primary propulsion system consists of a pair of electrospray thrusters providing a combined thrust of 0.064 mN at 1 W. The attitude control system consists of sun sensors, magnetometers, gyroscopes for attitude sensing and micro pulsed plasma thrusters for attitude correction. The mission consists of two phases. In Phase I, a 4U CubeSat is deployed from a 414 km orbit and uses the primary propulsion system to deorbit to a mean target altitude of 244 km. Phase I lasts 12.73 days with the propulsion system consuming 5.6 g of propellant to deliver a ∆𝑽𝑽 of 28.12 m/s. In Phase II the mission is maintained till remaining 25.2 g of propellant is consumed. Phase II lasts for 54.2 days, corresponding to a ∆𝑽𝑽 of 57.22 m/s.

record.title: A Multi-University Small Satellite Design Course : Systems Engineering Approach
record.abstract: This paper will review the technical outcomes of a unique two-semester graduate-level Small Satellite Systems Design Course, offered under a collaboration between North Carolina A&T, Old Dominion University, Georgia Tech and Florida Institute of Technology, with additional faculty support from Hampton University and NASA Langley Research Center. The course provided students with skills that are relevant to present day satellite design while fostering an open-ended mission design assignment that is relevant to the support of Earth observation using systems of small satellites. Major outcomes of this course include that the students have the experience of working in multi-disciplinary, multi-university teams, practicing critical thinking skills, and managing the design of complex systems. In addition, the course was developed around utilizing Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) practices and tools throughout the design life-cycle while utilizing a common design language, Systems Modelling Language (SysML). The approach started with a mission idea and proceeded to a feasible concept that included requirements development and management, concept modeling and performance simulation, and prototype building using low-cost additive manufacturing techniques, ending with a “Shark-tank” style presentation.

Results are presented using as many as 16384 processors on the Blue Waters and Titan supercomputers.

record.title: Centralized Autonomous Relative Navigation of Multiple Spacecraft Around Small Bodies
record.abstract: This paper presents an on-board, centralized autonomous navigation algorithm able to reconstruct the trajectories of a fleet of CubeSats relative to an asteroid binary system. The algorithm is executed on-board the main spacecraft, which takes relative measurements using a narrow optical camera and an additional relative measurement, being inter satellite ranging in this paper. The image processing algorithm detects and tracks the CubeSats, deriving line-of-sight measurements. A non-linear estimation filter is employed to reconstruct the trajectory. The algorithm is tested using high-fidelity trajectory simulator and synthetic images generation routines.

record.title: Using a Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) Variant Approach for Architecting Signal Processing in a Space-Based Sensor
record.abstract: Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) can be used to develop the architecture of a space-based sensor. The process begins with the development of use cases (UCs) of a general system model for a sensor processor which is composed of both hardware and software-based elements. Domain-specific UC?s can then be created and linked to the general level. This process continues through the modeling of variances in system behavior, including activity, sequence and state diagrams. This is done in parallel with the development of structural model instances that represent the configuration of the system for the specific domain being considered. The result is an end-to-end extensible sensor model that can then be applied to analyze the end-to-end signal processing chain.

record.title: A scheduling optimization using greedy knapsack algorithm for RANDEV CubeSat communication and observation missions analyzed with MBSE Activity Diagram
record.abstract: Repeater Arrangement & Disaster Early View (RANDEV) is a 3U CubeSat whose payloads are hyper-spectral camera, S-band receiver, and X-band transmitter. RANDEV conducts an earth observation mission to collect potential hazard image data from volcanoes, coasts, and clouds. The antennas are used to conduct store & forward and satellite internet missions. The concept of operations (CONOPS) of RANDEV is organized using top-down approach, and the top of the CONOPS is defined to ?Operation? which is comprised of ?Modes?. A Mode consist of ?Behaviors?, and they are composed of ?Actions?. The Actions are the bottom of the RANDEV missions, and defined by SysML Activity Diagram in language. The Actions are function names of RANDEV subsystem softwares. The time consumption of software functions is estimated using the activity diagram, and in order to practice three missions, a time scheduling methodology is proposed using greedy-knapsack algorithm in this research.

record.title: Effectiveness of CubeSat-Based Architectures for Active Removal of On-Orbit Rocket Bodies
record.abstract: Recent events such as the 2009 Iridium-Cosmos collision and multiple anti-satellite weapon (ASAT) tests have propelled the increasingly urgent topic of space debris management to the forefront of current engineering inquiry. Simultaneously, the so-called ?CubeSat Revolution? has significantly reduced barriers to entry for commercial and scientific space missions. Cube- Sats have demonstrated an ever-increasing potential to offer useful capabilities for a fraction of the size, mass, and power of their larger counterparts. This paper explores the relevance and effectiveness of CubeSat architectures in active space debris removal by propulsive methods. The chosen target of interest is the Zenit-2 second-stage rocket body, representative of a particularly large and prevalent family of debris objects. The debris removal mission design problem is approached from a fundamental level. First, the CubeSat architecture design tradespace is defined and outlined, including the proposed design vector, constraints, and objective function. Next, a system model and optimization methods are presented and implemented in MATLAB. Given a set of mission requirements, the algorithm arrives at an optimal or near-optimal architecture design by iterating through combinations of commercially available CubeSat components stored in a database. Results are examined for various deorbiter CubeSat designs, and key tradeoffs between architecture options are identified and explored. Finally, considering the optimized results, a discussion of the most effective propulsive solutions for Zenit-2 rocket body removal using CubeSat clusters is presented.

record.title: Programmatic Management for the ABEX CubeSat in a Model Based System Engineering Environment
record.abstract: View Video Presentation: https://doi.org/10.2514/6.2021-0623.vidThis paper describes how the systems engineering team has applied a Model Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) methodology to the Alabama Burst Energetics eXplorer (ABEX) project, formerly known as the Alabama Experiment for In-situ Shielding (AEGIS). The MBSE approach is based around the development of an Integrated Systems Model (ISM) that contains a model of the system and most of the programmatic information about the project. This paper details how the programmatic aspects of the projects were adapted to be recorded and tracked in the ISM.

record.title: Creating Future Space Technology Workforce Utilizing CubeSat Platforms: Challenges, Good Practices, and Lessons Learned
record.abstract: View Video Presentation: https://doi.org/10.2514/6.2021-1437.vidThe United States Naval Academy?s Small Satellite Program (NASSP) has been actively developing and launching space payloads since 2001 and has involved hundreds of undergraduate students in the design, development, integration, testing, and operation aspects of space systems engineering. NASSP has launched 17 space payloads so far, including seven CubeSats, with two more manifested for launch in 2021. The Naval Academy is an undergraduate-only institution, and thus has fostered a satellite engineering program centered around projects that were purely managed and run by students. NASSP and its space system projects have become more mature and streamlined over the years where the current Capstone Design operation is very close to achieving a ?One CubeSat a Year? model. The goal is to realize a streamlined design curriculum where the students will be able to experience the entire scope of a satellite system project cycle, from concept design to launch and operation. This paper will describe the challenges that such a program faces, discuss good practices learned along the way, and detail some lessons learned.

record.title: EPS TDS Electric Power Systems Time Dependent Simulation Tools For Verification, Validation, and Prediction
record.abstract: View Video Presentation: https://doi.org/10.2514/6.2021-3258.vidA group of computer code simulation tools has been created to predict the time dependent behavior of electrical power systems used in aerospace and satellite applications. These tools can also be used to simulate accurate power systems behavior in virtually all other power system applications and architectures, including vehicles, aircraft, solar powered facilities, power plants, and nuclear generating stations. It is important to note that although these tools can be used in many classified or secure areas, that the models and codes themselves as written and coded are not classified. Only the input and output data used in the codes could be considered to be classified. Also, many models that can be used in the codes may be considered to be proprietary. Any such models or data would then be allowed to be used only by those agencies that have legal access to that proprietary data. Generic models and user generated models can also be used wherever necessary.

record.title: EssentialSAT: A Space Systems Engineering Learning Laboratory
record.abstract: View Video Presentation: https://doi.org/10.2514/6.2022-4207.vidAs the space industry expands to include start-up companies and emerging space nations, there is pressing need for technical workforce development. Paper-based ?book learning? only takes us so far. Real hardware and software behave differently than models predict. The EssentialSAT desktop space system was developed to address this challenge. This low-cost, desktop satellite simulator system provides a unique, hands-on learning experience as a part of an integrated space systems engineering curriculum. EssentialSAT provides an educational kit of representative spacecraft subsystems that can be assembled, integrated, and tested in the classroom with simple ground support equipment. The discussion of EssentialSAT development highlights the application of an integrated digital ecosystem that includes CAD, eCAD, addictive manufacturing and all orchestrated using model-based systems engineering (MBSE). Its use as part of a classroom experience that allows students to learn about individual spacecraft subsystems?power, data handling, communication, attitude determination and control, remote sensing, mechanisms?as well as the assembly, integration and verification and operation of the entire system. The paper describes details of the system elements and interfaces. Conclusions describe describe future applications and its potential available as an open-source design.

record.title: Leveraging a Digital Engineering Testbed to Explore Mission Resilience for New Observing Strategies
record.abstract: View Video Presentation: https://doi.org/10.2514/6.2023-0257.vidThis study introduces the New Observing Strategies Testbed (NOS-T); a digital engineering environment to conduct coordinated experiments between independent and potentially geographically distributed nodes. The testbed supports both real-time applications and scaled-time simulations. NOS-T is built on an event-driven architecture where applications communicate via message payloads mediated by an event-broker. This allows for collaboration across organizational boundaries while maintaining autonomy and control over the flow of information. Testbed capabilities are demonstrated for an example problem exploring data downlink opportunities for two distinct ground network systems. A twenty-four hour mission is simulated for two Earth observing satellites in sun-synchronous orbits, with various iterations of traditional single arctic ground stations with fixed cost contracts versus newer commercial ground stations with on-demand cost models. Results demonstrate the capability of the commercial ground stations to maintain significant data margins throughout the mission with considerable cost-savings from the on-demand pricing.

record.title: Model-Based CubeSat Flight-Software Architecture using a Docs-as-Code approach
record.abstract: View Video Presentation: https://doi.org/10.2514/6.2023-1126.vidWith the growing community of CubeSat developers has emerged a need for a technical approach that would provide a means of fast-tracking the lifecycle development process of CubeSats, including the need to minimize design and development time repeating prior engineering efforts. In addition to a technical approach, there is also the need for a language and toolchain with a demand for both minimal training and minimal IT overhead to configure. A model-based approach has become a topic of interest in addressing much of these systems engineering painpoints. However, the current state-of-the-art tools demand either considerable investment in training and/or IT overhead, making it difficult for CubeSat developers of small startups or academia to participate. This article presents a model-based technical approach in conjunction with a docs-as-code approach, used to fascilitate flight software architecture development, intended to guide an implementation, for the SeaLion CubeSat mission - a joint CubeSat mission between the Old Dominion University and Coast Guard Academy. The technical approach discussed in this paper was also used to model and generate the paper as itself.

record.title: EarthScan-TSS, a Cubesat Based Tethered Satellite System And Platform To Test On Orbit Servicing And Space Sustainability
record.abstract: View Video Presentation: https://doi.org/10.2514/6.2023-1881.vidIn late 2026, sci_Zone in partnership with John Hopkins University is planning to deploy in Low Earth Orbit the EarthScan-TSS satellite to test on orbit servicing and space sustainability for the DoD, NASA and a range of commercial applications. The focus of the mission is to flight qualify a range of sensors and supporting software, Artificial Intelligence, and Autonomy tools ? QuickSAT/VMS and SHERLOCK MD ? that supports vehicle servicing and fault management, extravehicular assessment, local and global situational awareness and secondary vehicle characterization. The architecture will track data in an on board data lake using a hybrid Trustless Ledger System. For ease of payload repurposing EarthScan-TSS will utilize the flight qualified QuickSAT/Xen Space Hypervisor, a bare metal hypervisor that provides for secure isolation and protection of virtual payloads installed on on-orbit vehicles. QuickSAT/Xen also allows for payload repurposing isolated from the rest of the flight management system. The first phase of the mission is for two years in LEO at an altitude of 600 km to exercise a range of mission goals including a broad range of servicing and autonomy functions. The second phase of the mission will be to deploy a 24U cubesat from the main satellite on a 2 km tether to test a range of secondary vehicle monitoring functions over the controlled deployment and tether operations phases. We will also conduct a de-orbit maneuver using sci_Zone?s proprietary tether design and tether deployer system. For this presentation the mission design will be presented along with the baseline satellite design including both the primary and secondary elements plus the tether system. We will also cover the architecture of the QuickSAT/VMS system, SHERLOCK MD, and QuickSAT/Xen.

record.title: Using Small Satellites to Construct an In-Space Test Platform for Risk Reduction
record.abstract: View Video Presentation: https://doi.org/10.2514/6.2023-2214.vidTo overcome the technical readiness levels (TRL) 4 ? 7 ?Valley of Death? and accelerate new technology development, the US Space Force (USSF) started an in-Space Developmental Test (iSDT) initiative with its instantiation of a persistent iSDT platform called the Advanced Space-Based Testbed (XST). For risk-reduction, a scaled-down Mini-XST is proposed for proof-of-concept. Its key space systems include the spacecraft bus, test payloads, tender servicer to deliver test payload to the Mini-XST spacecraft, and robotic servicer to attach test payloads to the Mini-XST platform. In this paper, the proposed Mini-XST taking advantage of recent proliferated small satellite technologies as well as standard interface to support its successful operation will be discussed and illustrated.

record.title: The Economic Case for an Orbital Satellite Factory
record.abstract: In-Space Servicing, Assembly and Manufacturing (ISAM) is part of the United States National Strategy and an essential piece of future space architectures. Manufacturing on orbit is one of the elements of ISAM that requires significant investment and research. There is wide interest from government actors, as demonstrated by DARPA?s NOM4D project and NASA?s upcoming OSAM-1 and OSAM-2 efforts, and from venture-backed companies that are working to develop, demonstrate, and spur economic growth in ISAM. A novel Orbital Satellite Factory (OSF) concept is introduced that would autonomously manufacture and assemble small satellites in LEO from a persistent platform. The intent of this effort is to use the OSF concept as a notional reference architecture to identify critical capabilities and enabling technologies for ISAM applications, via an OSF technology roadmap. In an effort to better understand the value proposition of the OSF concept, this paper will (1) postulate a variety of use cases for the capabilities enabled by the orbital factory and its underlying technologies; and (2) develop a method to quantify the economic case for OSF using a notional satellite manufacturing scenario. We find that, though the OSF business case is initially weak, several sensitivities exist which can improve this picture ? among these are initial government investment/assistance, the target market of manufacturable satellites, and the total addressable demand for on-orbit manufactured satellites.

record.title: Digitally-assisted Development of a Space Robotic Arm for Small Satellites Applications
record.abstract: In-space servicing, assembly, and manufacturing (ISAM) expands space-based capabilities by extending satellite lifespans and decoupling spacecraft design from launch vehicle constraints. Robotic systems are proposed to support multiple aspects of ISAM missions, from capture and manipulation to manufacturing and repair. Consequently, the rapid development and testing of diverse robotic platforms is imperative to meet the evolving demands of the new space enterprise. This paper proposes a digital engineering framework to expedite the design, development, testing, and operation analysis of space robotic platforms. Digital engineering design tools are employed to optimize design for space environment operations; additionally, traditional manufacturing methods are streamlined with integrated wireless communication; IoT (Internet of thing) capabilities enable cloud-based modification to adjust to dynamic design requirements. Leveraging Amazon Web Services cloud-based servers, a digital twin of the robotic arm will be developed to assist the project's life cycle, from design to evaluation and test. AWS IoT communication protocols enable near real-time transmission of robotic arm sensor data to its digital twin. Siemens NX CAE (Computer Aided Engineering) facilitates photorealistic physics-based simulation, optimizing robotic arm control and motion planning. The paper details the digital engineering implementation of a two-degree-of-freedom robotic arm featuring piezoelectric rotary motors, applied in a zero gravity simulation air-bearing table study.

record.title: Wildfire Identification Via CMOS Sensor Fitted High-Altitude Long Endurance (HALE) System
record.abstract: Abstract Wildfires cause millions of dollars of damage each year and affect countless lives and habitats. Because of this, wildfire monitoring techniques have become necessary to protect property and natural ecosystems. Advances in Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) have allowed for safer, more cost-effective monitoring systems of forest fires. A constellation of high-altitude long-endurance (HALE) fixed-wing aircraft, such as the Airbus Zephyr S, with a camera system designed to detect forest fires, could be used to monitor high-risk wildfire areas constantly. The challenges of wildfire surveillance, such as aircraft type, altitude, search patterns, number of aircraft, and wind speed are reviewed to create a concept of operations for using a HALE UAS to detect wildfires. Additionally, a camera system capable of detecting wavelengths of light emitted by burning potassium in plant matter will be analyzed as a possible solution to current multispectral sensor system challenges when attempting to detect wildfire sources. A proof of concept of this system has been designed. Likewise, an apparatus designed to test a prototype version of this camera system has been created.

record.title: A Hosted Payload Cyber Attack Against Satellites
record.abstract: The increased utilization of small satellites, particularly CubeSats, has been propelled by technological advancements and the widespread incorporation of Commercial Off-The-Shelf (COTS) components. This transition has ushered in a paradigm of faster and more cost- effective missions, giving rise to novel trends such as the Internet of Space Things (IoST) and Space as a Service (SaaS) in the space domain. However, this shift comes with a concomitant rise in spacecraft architecture complexity, expanding the attack surface for potential cyber threats. Despite these advancements, space cybersecurity has lagged behind, largely adhering to traditional security-through-obscurity approaches, thereby endangering the security of future missions and critical infrastructure. This work delves into the OPS-SAT mission as a case study, presenting one of the most advanced CubeSat missions to date. OPS-SAT introduces innovative mission capabilities and novel concepts in space operations. In this study, we assume the role of malicious users, crafting and executing a cyber attack against the primary payload of the OPS-SAT spacecraft, within an emulated environment. The success of the attack is scrutinized, and the resultant impacts across the system are systematically enumerated. The study culminates in a formalized representation of the attack using established threat modeling frameworks, including attack trees and the SPARTA matrix. This approach offers a comprehensive examination of the OPS-SAT mission?s susceptibility to cyber threats, providing insights that can inform future cybersecurity strategies for advanced small satellite missions.

record.title: Analysis of a Bank Control Guidance for Aerocapture at Uranus
record.abstract: We apply the Fully Numerical Predictor-corrector Aerocapture Guidance to capture a vehicle into orbit for a mission at Uranus. Using the Genesis flight mechanics simulation, we analyze both undispersed and dispersed trajectories in order to tune the guidance parameters. We then assess the performance of the guidance using Monte Carlo analyses. Properly accounting for the oblateness of Uranus within the guidance proves to be critical. We identify high-to-low density gradients as the cause of large target orbit misses. Intentionally targeting a steeper flight-path angle at entry interface mitigates the risk of exiting the atmosphere on a hyperbolic orbit. Finally, We deliver the guidance code and tuned parameters for integration into the Program to Optimize Simulated Trajectories II.

record.title: Autonomous Satellite Operational Mode Switching for Anomalies and Space Weather Effects Mitigation
record.abstract: Space weather can affect satellite mission performance, especially during space weather events where particle intensity increases drastically, inducing anomalies in subsystems such as sensors or in introducing unaccountable dynamics. In this work, an autonomous Satellite Control System (SCS) operational autonomous mode selection has been proposed to mitigate the effects of a space weather event, before, while, and after it has happened. Modeled as a disturbance to the system, at each time-iteration, the most effective mode will be selected to ensure the safety of the spacecraft, while mitigating the impact on the mission as much as possible.

record.title: Space Logistics Exploration Campaign Scenario Specification for SpaceNet
record.abstract: Space logistics analysis is a critical systems engineering function to ensure feasibility of space exploration campaigns starting from early design concepts and maturing to more detailed operational plans. SpaceNet is an existing simulation tool that evaluates propulsive feasibility based on impulsive maneuvers required to traverse the exploration network and logistical feasibility by comparing resource demands to sustain mission operations to the available mass and volume afforded by the exploration architecture. A SpaceNet scenario contains information about the exploration network, campaign objects (resources, demand models, and elements), and mission events that comprise a human space exploration campaign. Recent development created a SpaceNet scenario specification using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Schema, a declarative language that annotates and validates JSON documents, expanding options for scenario construction, sensitivity analysis and trade studies, and distributed evaluation across diverse computing platforms. A supporting open-source Python language library provides scenario object classes for scripting and automation. This paper provides a technical description of the updated SpaceNet scenario specification. An example application case models a Lunar sortie mission based on the Artemis 3 mission using SpaceNet. The exploration mission considers a crew of four who rendezvous with the human landing system in a near rectilinear halo orbit about Earth-Moon L2. Two crew members enter the lander, transfer to a low Lunar orbit, and descend to the Lunar South Pole for a seven-day surface exploration. After collecting Lunar samples, they ascend to low Lunar orbit, transfer to the halo orbit, rendezvous with the crew and service module, and return to Earth. Results verify propulsive feasibility of a baseline mission concept without considering resource demands, showing positive propellant margins in the launch vehicle, in-space stage, landing system, and service module.

record.title: Test and Evaluation Procedure to Develop a Digital Twin of the Sleeper-Sat
record.abstract: A Digital Twin (DT) is not just a collection of static digital models at the component level of a physical system but a dynamic entity that evolves in parallel with the physical system it mirrors. This evolution starts with physics-based or data-driven physics models representing the physical system and advances to Authoritative Virtualization or DT through continuous data assimilation and ongoing Digital Engineering Test and Evaluation processes. This paper aims to create a mathematical framework for the DE Test and Evaluation Process, which incorporates data assimilation to link physical and digital models, uncertainty quantification, uncertainty propagation, and DT calibration process. This framework will enable the DT to perform operations, control, decision-making, and predictions at scale. The framework will be implemented to develop the DT of the Sleeper-sat to analyze the Sleeper-sat's structural deformation during its deployment in space. The Sleeper-sat will be a variant of previously constructed Sleeper-sats from the Aerospace Center at UTEP. The DT of the Sleeper-sat will be capable of predicting and monitoring structural health during its space operations.

record.title: A Scalable System Architecture for CubeSat Test & Evaluation for Enhanced Mission Success
record.abstract: This research applies systems engineering methodology to optimization of a CubeSat Test and Evaluation program. Currently, over 50% of CubeSats fail to perform their intended mission, in large part, due to inadequate test and evaluation procedures prior to flight. This paper applies Systems Engineering principles to increase the robustness and effectiveness of CubeSat test and evaluation with the goal of reducing the failure rate of CubeSat missions. This paper builds upon previous research to build the scalable systems architecture. The paper covers the set of model-based systems engineering diagrams and reports for the operational and logical/functional viewpoints of the CubeSat Test and Evaluation System.

record.title: Small Satellite Hybrid Propulsion Systems: A Numerical Strategy for Regenerative Cooling Design
record.abstract: With the rise of green propulsion systems alongside the growing need for an easier access to space by private aerospace companies and small satellite research groups, hybrid rocket engines start representing an attractive option for in-space propulsion because of their inherent advantages, such as safety, low toxicity, and low cost. However, challenges emerge in case of miniaturized engines requiring long-duration firings and/or multiple ignitions (as foreseen in different small satellite applications), since ablative passive thermal protection systems typically employed in the nozzle suffer excessive throat erosion and general thermal management issues. To address this, the present study proposes an efficient numerical approach for designing and analyze active regenerative cooling systems for small satellite hybrid propulsion, using carbon-based nozzles and liquid nitrous oxide (i.e., N2O) as coolant. The mathematical model proposed is firstly validated using data of an actively-cooled hybrid engine prototype recently tested at the Hokkaido University. The phase-change behavior of N2O is looked in details, and an evaporation rate law is proposed based on an ad-hoc reconstruction technique. Then, a simplified cooling system scalability study is carried out, underlining the potential advantages of a graphite-based liner over classical metal-based cooling jackets configurations. Lastly, an optimization algorithm for parametric design and optimization of the cooling system is introduced. The design algorithm is used to analyze two thrust-classes (≈100N and ≈1N) representative of hybrid engines in development at Letara Ltd., revealing that, while designing efficient cooling systems becomes more challenging with smaller engine scales, both engine scales can be successfully cooled using regenerative cooling methods, even considering manufacturing constraints related to 3D printing limits.

record.title: Digital Engineering for Cubesats With Semantic Web Technologies
record.abstract: Digital Engineering (DE) and the digital thread, which integrates information across the system lifecycle, offer transformative opportunities for systems engineering. This paper explores the application of DE principles to cubesat design and development, leveraging the Digital Engineering Factory (DEF) developed at the University of Arizona. The DEF integrates data from multiple engineering tools into a cohesive dataset using the Violet tool, which organizes the data as a graph database aligned with the University of Arizona Ontology Stack (UAOS). We extend prior work by applying the DEF to a cubesat design project. In particular, we develop a Python-based analysis to simulate orbital decay and calculate the time required for the cubesat to deorbit. This analysis uses inputs from multiple sources and is integrated into the workflow to demonstrate how the DEF supports automated traceability and checking of consistency, correctness, and completeness. This paper details the DEF's architecture, the cubesat application, and key findings, providing a pathway for advancing DE practices in cubesat design and development. Limitations and future research directions are discussed to guide further development of semantic web technologies in DE.

record.title: A Comparison of Bank Control and Direct Force Control for Aerocapture at Uranus
record.abstract: We compare bank angle control and direct force control for aerocapture at Uranus. We utilize the Fully Numerical Predictor-corrector Aerocapture Guidance for both configurations and discuss modifications to the direct force control corrector to handle multiple roots. Using the Genesis flight mechanics simulation, we analyze both nominal and dispersed three-degree-of-freedom trajectories with perfect navigation and control. We present Monte Carlo results and discuss differences between the performance of the two control approaches. We find that increased bank angle rate and acceleration limits do not increase the performance of the bank control configuration. We analyze a variation with tighter angle of attack bounds and find that the tuning and performance of the two configurations converges, because direct force control is less able to modulate drag.

record.title: A Model-Based Tool for Anomaly Management
record.abstract: MAGE formalizes a largely informal and experience-led decision-making process in small satellite anomaly management. It is especially useful when only limited telemetry data is available or novice groups of engineers, such as small-satellite university programs, encounter anomalies. These groups tend to be resource constrained in schedule, budget, and expertise. By leveraging hybrid model-based methods and logical reasoning, MAGE provides a structured, formalized, high-level approach to fault detection, diagnosis, and resolution that can be navigated effectively by novice and experienced operators. This comprehensive method extends beyond traditional fault trees, addressing the limitations posed by incomplete information and the potential biases of past experiences. The classification of anomalies is especially useful for understanding and resolving them. An existing spacecraft mission was used to validate MAGE. The results of which illustrate the practical application and benefits of MAGE, showcasing its ability to work with abstract models and limited data. Thus, this tool enables novice teams to manage spacecraft anomalies and potentially save their missions from failure. The versatility of MAGE and its integration of operator intent further enhance its utility, making it a valuable tool to ensure the success and reliability of future space missions.

record.title: Comparative Performance of Entry Simulations Using Guided Human-Scale Landers at Mars
record.abstract: There has been ongoing interest in human exploration of Mars since the 1970s. Most studies to date have investigated moderate lift-to-drag ratio vehicles to investigate this problem. This paper considers the development and cross-simulation comparison of a slender-bodied, moderate lift-to-drag human-scale lander vehicle for Mars. The vehicle employs the Fully Numerical Predictor-corrector Entry Guidance to target a powered descent state, subsequently leveraging Fractional Polynomial Powered Descent Guidance laws to reach the desired touchdown target. Differences in simulation environment as well as nominal trajectory results are shared.

record.title: Sliding Mode Control With Chattering Reduction
record.abstract: Sliding Mode Control is a powerful nonlinear control methodology that can handle parametric uncertainties and external disturbances. However, the discontinuous and high-frequency switching nature of the control law introduces the chattering phenomenon, which leads to potential actuator degradation, alterations to the desired response characteristics and, sometimes, instability during control implementation. The main objective of this paper is to study Sliding Mode Control with chattering reduction. The Sliding Mode Control law involves an equivalent control component and a discontinuous control component. A disturbance estimation is performed based on Lyapunov analysis and adaptive control techniques and then included in the Sliding Mode Control law as part of the equivalent control term. As a result, the Sliding Mode Control gain could be set to a smaller constant value so as to reduce chattering. The modified controller is tested on a simulation model of the rotational dynamics of a small satellite experiencing constant disturbances using quaternion kinematics and Euler?s equations of rotational motion. Furthermore, a Conventional Sliding Mode Controller and an Adaptive Controller are also designed using Lyapunov analysis. The error quaternion and angular velocities are driven towards the identity quaternion and zero respectively using all three control methods and a comparative analysis of the results obtained is conducted.

record.title: Formulation of an Uncertainty Analysis Methodology for Computational Fluid Dynamics of External Flows Over Launch Vehicles
record.abstract: Space launch vehicles are often engineered with large safety factors due to the scarcity and cost of ground tests. In addition, these vehicles often carry expensive and delicate payloads that must go through extreme launch conditions. Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) can be utilized to support the design of these vehicles but often have uncertainty and errors associated with them that are often not fully quantified. This paper provides a methodology and investigation for quantifying and estimating the uncertainty for CFD over space launch vehicles when no experimental data exists. A generic launch vehicle was used for this study. The primary output quantities of interest for the study are the aerodynamic coefficients. While there are numerous sources of uncertainty, this study investigates the impact of mesh quality, boundary conditions, and turbulence models. The largest uncertainty lies in the y-moment coefficient, where the y-axis is aligned with the angle of attack, and is due to perturbing the turbulence model for a zero-degree angle of attack configuration or perturbing the mesh quality for a six-degree angle of attack configuration. The smallest uncertainty is in the x-moment coefficient, with a zero percent uncertainty for all configurations.

record.title: Multidisciplinary Optimization and Experimental Aerodynamic Assessment of a Crew Return Vehicle
record.abstract: The aim of the present paper is to study the preliminary aeroshape design and low-speed aerodynamic analysis of a crew reentry vehicle for low-earth orbit servicing. An in house, well-established multi-disciplinary design optimization procedure has been employed to assess several aeroshape candidates. Once the main goals and requirements for the mission are provided, the optimization procedure can identify the optimal configuration of the Crew Return Vehicle, plus some alternate plausible variants. In order to efficiently manage parametric design components, a proprietary Skeleton-based Integral Soft Object methodology has been integrated and employed in the optimization framework. The final candidates are mainly differentiated by a specific design for the configuration of the winglets and vertical tails (single vertical tail vs. V-tail). Subsequently, a wind tunnel test campaign has been carried out in the 4x3 ft low-speed wind tunnel at the School of Aeronautical Engineering of the University of Sydney to validate low-speed aerodynamic behavior related to landing conditions. In this work, longitudinal and lateral-longitudinal aerodynamic performance of the NM3 candidate configuration is analyzed and discussed.

record.title: Advancing the SmallSat Digital Twin for Active Debris Removal Simulations
record.abstract: The growing density of orbital debris threatens active spacecraft and future missions. While nets, harpoons, and robotic arms show promise for cleaning up debris, they are costly and demand precise control, motivating interest in space-based lasers that use ablation to impart small velocity changes for just-in-time collision avoidance and deorbiting. To mature this approach, we extend the SmallSat Digital Twin (SSDT) to provide a high-fidelity, spacecraft-focused simulation that integrates avionics, dynamics, core Flight System (cFS) flight software, ground control (OpenC3), and new radar/optical sensor and debris models. The enhanced SSDT supports realistic detection logic (Sun/Earth exclusion, field of view, limiting magnitude), representative tumbling debris with size/reflectivity parameters, and a laser engagement model based on an impulsive momentum transfer.

record.title: Attitude Determination for Nanosattelites
record.abstract: Abstract Nanosatellites are becoming more relevant due to their low-cost ability to complete missions previously reserved for larger satellites. Due to growing interest in this field of technology, the need for attitude determination systems in transmission, Intelligence Survey and Reconnaissance, and other essential satellite reliant industries has become much more prevalent. Attitude determination is a first step towards proper attitude control, which is a gateway to more complex technological advances. A system utilizing a Quaternion Multiplicative Extended Kalman Filter to fuse a multitude of sensors propagated over time, provides accurate attitude determination. Sensors include: two Commercial Off the Shelf gyroscopes, magnetometers, a custom sun sensor, and a small camera that doubles as a star tracker and earth horizon sensor. Furthermore, Accurate position tracking data is obtainable using a Precise Orbit Determination Extended Kalman Filter to ingest raw GPS observables and output filtered position and velocity.

record.title: A Steam Engine for the Space Age: Thermodynamic Analysis of a Detonation Thruster With Water Electrolysis Propellant Generation
record.abstract: A thermodynamic model of a water electrolysis system is developed and integrated into a thermodynamic system model of a detonative combustion engine to enable the analysis of theoretical small-spacecraft detonation propulsion systems using water electrolysis for propellant generation. Due to the additional time required to generate propellants via electrolysis, these thrusters lend themselves well to infrequent, impulsive firings rather than sustained burns. Performance characteristics including specific impulse, energy efficiency, and a theoretical maximum impulse are identified for a representative nanosatellite-class spacecraft thruster with ideal and nonideal detonation combustion operation using an annular combustor with a plug nozzle and compared to deflagration operation using a traditional converging-diverging nozzle. The volume savings from stored liquid water propellant are also quantified compared to compressed gas tanks with equivalent thruster performance, with some configurations representing a volume reduction of multiple orders of magnitude. Results suggest that the in-space detonation thruster architectures characterized in this analysis are potentially attractive for applications such as station-keeping or orbital transfers.

record.title: Multidisciplinary Co-Design Optimization and Reinforcement Learning for CubeSat Architecting
record.abstract: Preliminary design stage of aerospace system presents a challenge to rapidly evaluate architectural selections with acceptable accuracy. Several actors involve at this stage, such as mission owner, mission designer, and technology provider. The cooperation among these actors promote co-design activities. Co-design means parts of the design are performed by "ideal" sizing models (physics- and mission-based), while the other parts leverage the flight heritage or commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) components. However, there is barely research exploring co-design concept in both component and analysis levels using Multidisciplinary Design Optimization (MDO) technique. Therefore, we propose a framework to formulate multidisciplinary co-design optimization in these levels for CubeSat architecting. The framework is capable to quantify the impacts of integrating COTS components into an "ideally-designed" CubeSat. The results show that some COTS perform comparably as high as the ideal design, while the others do not. The performance properties (e.g. power architecture score and CubeSat mass) provide some insights to actors to decide which components are suitable to be on-board. Based on those properties, the importance of each architectural decision-making is deducted quantitatively. Then, we implement reinforcement learning (RL) into the framework to explore the design space and find the optimum CubeSat architectures. The results show that RL is advantageous compared to enumerative approach for larger number of CubeSat architectures. Both mission designer and technology provider can leverage the framework to reduce the duration of architectural decision-making during preliminary design stage.

record.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Safe Satellite Operational Mode Switching
record.abstract: Space weather phenomena can degrade satellite mission efficacy, particularly during space weather events where their magnitude intensifies significantly and unexpectedly. This research proposes a smart Satellite Control System (SCS) operational mode selection framework using a deep Dyna-Q algorithm, designed to mitigate the effects of space weather events and also enhance overall mission efficiency in real-time. The reinforcement learning agent selects the optimal operational mode between three modes: orbit transfer, orbit correction, and the safe hold mode. The decision-making process is carried out to maximize the reward function, which is defined to incorporate space weather health risks due to radiation in conjunction with mission performance metrics, such as tracking precision, promptness, and fuel consumption, among others.

record.title: K-ADEPT: Modeling the Hypersonic Reentry of an Innovative Thermal Protection System
record.abstract: The ADEPT TPS is an innovative TPS scheme developed by NASA Ames Research Center. This TPS scheme will be mounted to a KRUPS capsule in the upcoming KREPE-3 mission. This study performed CFD simulations using the KATS-FD flow solver. CAD modeling software was used to produce high fidelity 2D and 3D CFD meshes. Cases were run with 55.0 km and 52.5 km flow conditions taken from the KREPE-1 mission. Heat flux maps were produced which show distributions due to shockwave interactions.

record.title: Applying Program Theory Innovation Model for ECLSS Development for India?s Gaganyaan Human Space Flight Program
record.abstract: The Indian Space Research Organization (ISRO) implements the national space activities under the policy direction of the Space Commission constituted within the Department of Space (DoS), Government of India that directly reports to the Prime Minister of India. The stated vision of ISRO is to ?Harness, sustain and augment space technology for national development, while pursuing space science research and planetary exploration.? Over the past five decades, ISRO has established India as a leading spacefaring nation through the Indian Remote Sensing (IRS) satellites program for civilian earth observation and disaster management, the Indian National Satellites (INSAT) program for telecommunications and broadband network, Navigation with Indian Constellation (NavIC), and through dedicated planetary and astronomy space science missions. In 2018, the Indian government committed the nation to pursuing human spaceflight with a budget allocation of ?10,000 Crores (~ $1.4 billion) and subsequently provide a net additional funding of ?11,170 Crore in 2024, with the objective to spur R&D in the nation and enable India to participate in future global space exploration endeavors for national benefits. In January 2019, ISRO established the Human Space Flight Center (HSFC) and is currently embarking on an ambitious ?Gaganyaan? program to realize human spaceflight capabilities within the nation, to undertake a crewed mission by 2027-28 to carry a crew of up to three to Low Earth Orbit (LEO) for up to three days and return them safely to Indian sea waters and from 2028 to begin missions to establish the Indian Space Station, ?Bharatiya Antariksh Station? (BAS), in a circular Low Earth Orbit (LEO) of about 400-450 km by 2035. The Environmental Control and Life Support Systems (ECLSS) that provides a safe and habitable environment for Crew Health & Performance (CHP) in the harsh conditions of space is the most critical component for any human spaceflight (HSF) mission. The development of ECLSS is a strategic capability in the space domain that only a few countries have achieved. In this paper, I provide the stakeholder & technical requirements and the structure of the major ECLSS subsystems through MBSE SysML diagrams. Given the significance and novel nature of ECLSS development for India?s emerging human spaceflight program, I then applied the innovation model from program theory to develop and understand the outcomes chain for the ECLSS Innovation.

record.title: On-Orbit Digital Twin for Spacecraft Battery State and Health Estimation
record.abstract: Lithium-ion batteries are mission-critical for nearly every modern spacecraft, yet their on-orbit management remains dominated by conservative, heuristic flight rules that sacrifice usable energy and operational flexibility to avoid degradation. This paper presents a lightweight battery digital-twin framework built around a dual extended Kalman filter (Dual-EKF) coupled with an equivalent-circuit model. A fast filter tracks state of charge (SOC) at every measurement sample, while a slow filter estimates capacity for real-time state-of-health (SOH) monitoring. On-board battery capacity forecasts are correlated with periodic reference performance tests (RPTs) and compared to the digital twin prediction. The framework is validated in the laboratory on EEMB LIR-2032 coin cells and currently on orbit aboard the Proteus Space Mercury One spacecraft, which carries a dedicated cycling payload with three Li-ion coin cells. Ground testing achieves a voltage-prediction RMSE below 5 mV and capacity estimation within 2% of RPT-derived values; preliminary on-orbit results show consistent SOC convergence, capacity-fade trends in line with ground priors, and graceful behavior under telemetry dropouts. We also outline a short future-work direction: a Gaussian-process-based lithium plating detector that would add degradation-mechanism awareness to the digital twin, enabling operators to distinguish aging from damaging plating events.

record.title: Reliability-Oriented Optimization of a Command-and-Control System for Advanced Air Mobility
record.abstract: Reliability engineering plays a critical role in ensuring safe operations in Advanced Air Mobility (AAM). This study presents a system-level optimization framework for evaluating and improving the reliability of a generic Command-and-Control (C2) system architecture based on the Mobile Testing and Evaluation Center (MTEC) unit developed by Parallax Advanced Research. The C2 architecture is decomposed into several primary subsystems, including power, communication, sensing, control (hardware and software), and data storage, allowing reliability to be evaluated at both the subsystem and overall system levels. The optimization model aims to maximize total system reliability, sensor detection probability, and detection range by modifying the sensing and control subsystems. The sensing subsystem includes six sensor types: radar, radio frequency (RF), Automatic Dependent Surveillance?Broadcast (ADS-B), acoustic sensors, Remote Identification (Remote ID), and optical cameras. The baseline control subsystem consists of eight primary workstations capable of supporting up to 20 UAVs. Additional workstations can be incorporated to improve overall system reliability. The decision variables include the number of sensors of each type and the number of additional workstations added to the control subsystem. The objective function maximizes system reliability, detection probability, and detection range while satisfying budget constraints and a minimum reliability requirement of 95%. The model is evaluated across budgets ranging from $30,000 to $150,000 and UAV fleet sizes from 20 to 50 vehicles. For a representative scenario with 20 UAVs and a $60,000 budget, the optimal configuration includes four backup workstations, sixteen ADS-B sensors, one Remote ID sensor, and one optical camera. This configuration achieves approximately 97% system reliability at a total cost of $59,793.80. The results demonstrate that both system budget and fleet size significantly influence reliability and optimal resource allocation.
